title: feat(smtp): DNSBL connection-time IP blocklist + DNSWL whitelist
description:
## Why

DNS Blocklists (DNSBLs) reject known spam-source IPs before a single byte of the SMTP conversation is read. One DNS lookup per connection, at accept() time. Spamhaus ZEN alone covers the majority of spam-sending IPs. Cost is negligible once the DNS cache (41l0/cs5p) is in place.

## How DNSBLs work

To check whether `1.2.3.4` is listed in `zen.spamhaus.org`:
- Reverse the IP octets: `4.3.2.1`
- Look up `4.3.2.1.zen.spamhaus.org` as an A record
- If it resolves (any 127.x.x.x answer) → listed; the specific 127.x.x.x value encodes the list category
- If NXDOMAIN → not listed

IPv6: expand to full form, reverse nibbles, append zone.

## Design

### Config

```toml
[[dnsbl]]
zone = "zen.spamhaus.org"
action = "reject"      # "reject" | "defer" | "tag"

[[dnsbl]]
zone = "bl.spamcop.net"
action = "reject"

[[dnsbl]]
zone = "list.dnswl.org"   # whitelist: listed here = skip all blocklists
action = "whitelist"
```

Multiple zones supported; evaluated in order. First `whitelist` hit skips remaining checks. First `reject` hit closes the connection.

`action = "tag"` adds an `X-DNSBL-Hit: <zone>` header (passed to Sieve) without rejecting — useful for testing a new zone before trusting it.

### Hookup point

In `crates/smtp/src/server.rs`, after `accept()` and before `tokio::spawn(run_session(...))`:

```rust
if let Some(verdict) = dnsbl_check(&auth_resolver, &config.dnsbl, peer_addr.ip()).await {
    match verdict {
        DnsblVerdict::Reject(zone) => {
            // send 554, drop connection — no session spawned
            let mut stream = ...;
            stream.write_all(b"554 5.7.1 ... blocked\r\n").await.ok();
            drop(permit);
            continue;
        }
        DnsblVerdict::Tag(zone) => { /* carry zone name into run_session */ }
        DnsblVerdict::Whitelist => { /* skip greylist, skip further DNSBL */ }
    }
}
```

`auth_resolver` is the existing `Arc<MessageAuthenticator>` — its hickory resolver handles the DNSBL A lookups.

### Implementation

`dnsbl_check(resolver, zones, ip) -> Option<DnsblVerdict>`:
1. Construct the lookup name: reverse IP + "." + zone
2. Call resolver A lookup (hickory, already async, TTL-cached)
3. Iterate zones in config order; return first hit

IPv4 reversal: `format!("{}.{}.{}.{}.{}", d, c, b, a, zone)` from `Ipv4Addr` octets.
IPv6: expand to 32 hex nibbles, reverse, join with `.`, append zone.

### Reject response

```
554 5.7.1 Service unavailable; Client host [1.2.3.4] blocked using zen.spamhaus.org
```
Per RFC 5321 §4.2, a 554 greeting rejection is legal before EHLO.

### DNSWL integration

`list.dnswl.org` (and `swl.spamhaus.org`) are whitelists: a hit means the IP is known-good. List these first with `action = "whitelist"` to bypass greylisting and skip remaining DNSBL checks for trusted senders.

### No default zones in code

The config ships with `dnsbl = []` (empty). Operators must opt in to specific zones. This avoids baking in third-party policy and ensures operators read the terms of service for each DNSBL they use (Spamhaus requires a data feed subscription for high-volume use).

## Acceptance criteria

- Listed IP receives 554 before EHLO
- Unlisted IP proceeds to normal session
- `action = "whitelist"` hit skips all subsequent blocklist checks
- `action = "tag"` hit does not reject; zone name available to session
- IPv4 and IPv6 lookup names constructed correctly (test vectors from Spamhaus docs)
- Empty `dnsbl = []` config: behaviour identical to today
- cargo fmt + clippy -D warnings + cargo test --workspace clean
notes: COORDINATION: stoa-1d9d418c (manual peer whitelist) and stoa-ef702cf6 (greylisting) share the same connection_whitelisted: bool parameter in run_session. Whichever of 1d63 or na4h lands first adds this parameter. The DNSWL whitelist hit (action='whitelist') sets connection_whitelisted=true. The manual peer whitelist (na4h) also sets it true on CIDR match. mgzn reads it to skip the greylist check. Before implementing, check whether na4h has already landed and added the parameter; if so, reuse it. The flag is a single bool — one parameter, two sources (DNSWL + manual CIDR), one consumer (greylisting).
design: hookup in server.rs after accept() before tokio::spawn; reuse Arc<MessageAuthenticator> hickory resolver for A lookups; no new DNS dependency. No default zones — operator opt-in only.
